"Fare" drops its "-e" before an infinitive: far ve-DE-re, far en-TRA-re.
1. Fare + infinitive: having someone do something
"Fare" + infinitive shows that you DON'T do the action yourself, but make it happen (you have someone else do it):
Will you show me the X-ray?
The person who actually does the action is introduced with "a" or "da": "Faccio smontare il ponteggio AGLI / DAGLI operai."
Pronouns go BEFORE "fare" (they don't attach to the infinitive). In the imperative, they attach to "fare":
I'm having it taken down on Thursday.
Show him in! Let him in!
NOT "Faccio smontarlo". You say "LO faccio smontare". The pronoun goes with "fare", not with the infinitive.
3. Farsi + infinitive: having something done to / for you
When someone else does something FOR YOU or TO YOU, use "farsi + infinitive". In the past, with ESSERE:
I have my hair cut (at the hairdresser's).
The minister wants to have his photo taken.
We let the whole of Ortigia help us.

Romanian says "mă tund" (I cut my hair), "îmi fac o rochie" (I make a dress), even though someone else does it. In Italian "Mi taglio i capelli" = I cut my own hair! At the hairdresser's: "Mi faccio tagliare i capelli" (like English "I have my hair cut").
4. Lasciare + infinitive: letting someone do something
"Lasciare" + infinitive = to allow. Pronouns behave as with "fare":
I'll let him speak for two minutes.
The difference: "Faccio entrare i bambini" (I decide they should come in, I call them) / "Lascio entrare i bambini" (they want to come in, I allow it).

On Sunday morning the cathedral square in Syracuse was full of people. Dr Russo had had a stage put up in front of the church, had had a thousand posters printed and had brought in two national TV channels. The minister, as expected, was late. "For once, we'll keep him waiting," Russo had said; after six months with Giulia, he had learned not to be afraid of the powerful any more.

Almost everyone had come. Graziella and Pietro had arrived from Florence on Friday; Ion and Doina, naturally, by train, after thirty-two hours of travelling, of which Ion had given a detailed account to anyone willing to listen. Assunta, on the other hand, had stayed in Naples: at ninety-two, she had said, you have the Caravaggios brought to your house, you don't go to the Caravaggios. Gennaro had promised to show her everything live on his phone.

The evening before, when the workers had finished taking down the scaffolding, Turi had let Matei and Giulia into the empty church and switched off all the lights except one. They had stood looking at the painting from the floor, for the first time in six months, with no ladders or lamps. "We'd never seen it like this from up here," Giulia had said. "From down here," Matei had corrected her. Turi had laughed softly and left them alone until midnight.

Concetta had had a blue dress made by the best dressmaker in Ortigia, and had had her hair done at the hairdresser's at six in the morning. She sat in the front row, as straight as a queen, with Viola on her knees. Turi, on the other hand, hadn't had anything new made. He wore his usual black suit, his Sunday one, and in his pocket was a sheet with his speech, which he had rewritten eleven times.

At eleven the schoolchildren came in, the ones with the drawings. Russo had had them line up two by two, but as soon as they saw the painting, freed from the scaffolding and lit as it had never been in four hundred years, the line broke up. They all ran forward, shouting. The teachers wanted to call them back, but Bellini raised a hand. "Let them run," he said. "It's for them that we did it."

The painting was transformed. Where before there had been a brown haze, now you could see Caravaggio's colours: the red of the cloak, the golden light on the gravediggers' shoulders, the pale face of the saint. Even the great dark void at the top seemed to breathe. And next to it, on the illuminated panel, was Totò's X-ray, with a small plaque: "Let him sleep. Ortigia is watching over him."

The minister arrived at ten to twelve, shook a lot of hands and gave a fifteen-minute speech in which he mainly thanked himself. Then he wanted to have his photo taken in front of the painting. Russo, with an innocent smile, had the children come closer. In every newspaper photo the next day, the minister appeared surrounded by sixty children holding up their drawings of Totò. Only his tie was visible.

Then it was Turi's turn. He climbed onto the stage trembling, took out the sheet, looked at it, and put it back in his pocket. "I wrote a speech," he said into the microphone in his hoarse voice. "But I'm not going to read it. I just wanted to say one thing. For fifty years I've been letting people into this church. This morning, for the first time, it was the church that let me in. Thanks to these youngsters, and thanks to you."

Nobody understood exactly what he meant, but everyone applauded for two minutes, and Concetta was crying so much she had to borrow a handkerchief from Graziella. Bellini didn't want to speak. "Let the young ones speak," he had told Russo. "I've talked enough for sixty-two years." So it was Matei and Giulia who climbed onto the stage, holding hands.

Giulia had only just begun to thank the city when something happened that nobody had foreseen. Viola, on Concetta's knees, began to wriggle. Concetta put her down on the marble floor, holding her hands. And Viola, who was ten months old and had never walked, broke free of Concetta's hands and took a step. Then another. Then another.

An absolute silence fell over the church. Three hundred people, a minister and two TV crews watched a ten-month-old baby walking, unsteadily, towards Caravaggio's painting. She took seven steps, stopped right below Totò's panel, raised her hand towards the X-ray, as if she wanted to wave to him, and sat down on the floor, very pleased with herself.

The applause that followed was the longest of the day, much longer than the applause for the minister. Giulia, on the stage, couldn't speak any more. Matei took the microphone and said only: "I think my daughter has just made the best speech. I have nothing to add." Then he stepped down from the stage and went to pick her up.

The party went on until evening on Concetta's terrace. Saro, the head of the fishermen, had had a crate of sea urchins brought over and had insisted on making Ion taste them; after the first one, Ion asked in Romanian whether it was legal to eat something like that. Pietro made everyone laugh by imitating the minister. And Viola, who no longer wanted to be held by anyone, let people hold her hands and walked from one table to another, as if she had always done it.

That evening, on the phone, Grandma Assunta, who had seen everything live thanks to Gennaro, said just one sentence: "I told you so, at Christmas. First tooth at Christmas, first steps in front of a masterpiece. Nothing will stop this little girl."
